nexus.html.title: A practical guide to the Nexus Grid word puzzle
nexus.html.body:
Nexus Grid is a word-grouping game: sixteen tiles belong to four groups, each with a connection you can describe. A connection might be a category, a shared expression, or another relationship between the words. Select four tiles and submit them together. Finding one plausible link is useful, but the complete solution has to make sense across all sixteen words.

Read the whole board before choosing

Look for a group whose four members fit equally well. Three strong matches and a fourth that needs a complicated explanation are a reason to pause. A word can suggest more than one group, so consider what your choice would leave behind. The final four tiles can help confirm whether an earlier idea was sound.

Use feedback to change the idea

A wrong submission uses an attempt. Reconsider the category rather than repeatedly changing one tile at random. You can shuffle the board to see the same words in a different arrangement, and deselect a group before submitting it. If you run out of guesses, reveal the solution and compare the intended connections with your own.

For more approaches, read How to Play Nexus Grid. If you enjoy word relationships, try Word Ladder or the clue-based Mini Crossword next.

cryptex.html.title: Use the letter clues in CryptEx
cryptex.html.body:
CryptEx asks you to solve a hidden five-letter word. The board gives feedback about correct positions and letters that belong elsewhere. Treat each attempt as a way to narrow the possibilities, rather than simply another chance to get lucky. You have six attempts, so the information from an early guess matters even when it is not the answer.

Separate a letter from its position

A letter can belong in the word while still occupying the wrong position. Keep that distinction in mind when planning the next guess. A confirmed position gives you a useful anchor; the remaining spaces are where you can test alternatives. Avoid spending another attempt on letters the feedback has already ruled out.

Check the whole candidate

Before submitting, compare your idea with every clue you have collected. Does it keep the known positions? Does it use the letters you still need to place? A word that fits the latest clue but contradicts an earlier one is unlikely to help. Repeated letters can also make a candidate look more promising than it is, so inspect each position separately.

Prefer a puzzle built around definitions? Try Mini Crossword. For a different letter challenge, Word Ladder asks you to connect two words one change at a time. The word and logic collection brings these games together.

mathsprint.html.title: How to approach a Math Sprint round
mathsprint.html.body:
Math Sprint presents an arithmetic expression and a choice of answers. Read the operation before choosing: a familiar pair of numbers can tempt you into answering an addition problem as though it were multiplication. The round timer adds pressure, but taking a moment to read clearly can be more useful than tapping the first plausible option.

Use a quick reasonableness check

For an addition, ask whether the answer should be larger than both positive terms. For subtraction, think about the size of the difference. Multiplication and division often become easier when you recall a related number fact. These checks can help reject a distractor, but they do not replace reading the exact expression.

Compare attempts fairly

Rounds can contain different questions, so two scores are not identical tests. A change in score may reflect the particular expressions, an interruption, or a mistap. Use the final correct and error counts as feedback about that round. The game is recreational and does not measure intelligence or establish a health benefit.

For a challenge with more time to think, try Tango Logic. For a short knowledge round, try Rapid Fire Trivia. You can read What a Game Score Means for more about interpreting results.

minigames.html.title: Set up a friendly game of Sketch and Guess
minigames.html.body:
Sketch and Guess is a team drawing activity. Use the screen to reveal a secret word and keep time; the drawing itself can happen on paper or on a whiteboard. One person sees the word and sketches it while their teammates guess. Keep the answer screen out of the guessing team's sight.

Agree on the drawing rules

Decide whether letters, numbers, gestures, and spoken hints are allowed before the first turn. A simple starting rule is pictures only, with no spelling out the answer. Choose a word category that both teams know and a time limit that suits the group. The setup screen lets you name the teams and choose the category and timer.

Keep the handover clear

When a turn ends, mark whether the word was guessed and pass the device to the next drawer. Give everyone a chance to draw. If a word is unfamiliar or a drawing causes a disagreement, agree on how to handle it together and use the same rule for both teams.

For a game without paper, try the same-device trivia duel. For a group answering on individual phones, visit hosted trivia. The quiz-night guide has ideas for pacing and mixing different formats.

rapid.html.title: How Rapid Fire Trivia works
rapid.html.body:
Rapid Fire is a timed quiz about a topic you choose. Start with sixty seconds and answer one multiple-choice question at a time. Correct answers build your score and your current streak; each wrong answer breaks that streak and removes five seconds from the remaining time. The clock keeps running while you switch tabs, so start when you have a minute to spend on the round.

Choose a familiar topic or try something new

The topic menu draws from the site's trivia banks. A round mixes the available difficulty levels for that subject, and the answer positions are shuffled. Read the entire question before choosing: a date, a name, or a word such as “not” can change what the question is asking. If you prefer to think without a timer, choose the untimed quiz link instead.

Use the controls that suit your device

Tap or click an answer, focus a button and press Enter or Space, or use the number keys 1–4 for the corresponding choices. One answer is accepted for each question. Brief feedback shows the correct answer before the next question appears. If you want to stop early, Finish this round saves the answers you have already submitted.

Review the result, rather than only the total

The result shows correct answers out of submitted answers, your longest correct-answer streak, and an expandable review. A question still on screen when the clock expires is not counted as an incorrect answer. An answered round earns 20 completion XP, plus 15 for each correct answer and 10 for each question in your best streak, up to 10,000 XP. A round with no answers earns no XP and adds no completion.

Question sets vary, so scores from different rounds are not identical comparisons. For a slower format, try the Daily Ten or an untimed science quiz. See What a Game Score Means for more about interpreting results.

timeline-history.html.title: Build a History Timeline, one event at a time
timeline-history.html.body:
History Timeline asks you to match historical events to dated positions. Select an event from the list, then select the slot where you think it belongs. Easy rounds contain six events, medium rounds eight, and hard rounds ten. You can take your time: the elapsed-time display is a record of the round, not a countdown that ends your attempt.

Begin with a date you recognise

Look at the earliest and latest dates before placing a card. An event you know well can anchor the rest of the timeline. Then think in relative order: did an invention appear before a familiar political event, or after it? If two positions share the same year, either event from that year fits either position. The game does not require an arbitrary order within a single year.

Change a placement before checking

Each event can occupy only one slot. Use the remove button on a placed card to return it to the list, or select another event for that position. Cards and empty slots can also be focused and activated with the keyboard. Place every event before choosing Verify Timeline. The feedback marks correct and incorrect placements so you can reconsider the mismatches.

What the result records

A fully solved easy round starts at 300 XP, medium at 500, and hard at 800. Each additional verification reduces that reward by 50 XP, with a minimum of 50. Repeatedly pressing Verify after a solved round does not create extra completions or XP. The result displays the number of checks and the elapsed time; your shared profile records one finished puzzle.

For a shorter historical comparison, try Which Came First?. For question-based history, visit History Trivia. The progress guide explains how finished games contribute to your profile.

hangman.html.title: Play Hangman with themed word collections
hangman.html.body:
This Hangman game uses words and phrases from themed collections. Choose a category or keep the mixed collection, then reveal the answer by guessing letters. Each incorrect new letter uses one of six allowed mistakes. A letter already chosen cannot cost another mistake, and a correct guess reveals every occurrence of that letter.

Use the word shape and the category

Read the category before choosing your first letter. Word length, visible spaces, and a familiar subject can narrow the possibilities. Punctuation and numbers are shown automatically: an apostrophe, a hyphen, or the digits in a title do not need to be entered on the letter keyboard. Guess only the letters A–Z.

Keyboard, touch, and hints

Use the on-screen letter buttons, or type a letter on a physical keyboard. Used letters are marked so you can see which guesses were hits and which were misses. The Hint button reveals the available hint for the current word. It does not take away a guess. When the word is solved or all mistakes are used, the result shows the complete answer and its description.

Word streaks and player progress

The word streak counts consecutive solved Hangman words and resets after a loss. It is separate from the profile's day streak. A solved word earns 50 XP plus 10 for each word in the current win streak, up to 10,000 XP. An unsuccessful word records the finished attempt with zero XP. The level and XP shown on this page now use the same player profile as the site header; individual letters do not add shared profile XP.

For clues instead of letter guesses, try Mini Crossword. For a one-letter-at-a-time path, try Word Ladder. The word and logic collection has more games to explore.
